subject: Cognitive Science
title: How Babies Build Categories
description: A quick win: understand How Babies Build Categories.

hook.text: Show a baby ten different cats, then show a dog. The baby stares longer. It noticed the switch.

buildup.text: This looking-time trick lets researchers measure categorization in infants who cannot speak.

discovery.text: By three months, babies distinguish animals from vehicles. By ten months, cats from dogs.

twist.text: They do this without anyone teaching labels. Categories form from pure perceptual experience.

climax.text: Language later sharpens these boundaries, but the raw groupings come first.

quiz.question: How do researchers study categorization in infants?
options: By measuring how long babies look at new items

details.summary: Infants begin categorizing the world within months of birth. By three months, they distinguish cats from dogs in looking-time studies. Babies use perceptual features first, then gradually add functional and causal knowledge. Category formation is a bootstrapping process from perception to theory.
details.whyItMatters: Infant categorization shows that the ability to group objects is not taught but is a fundamental cognitive capacity present from the earliest months of life.
takeaways: Infants categorize objects within the first months of life
Early categories are perceptual; later ones are theory-based
Labels and language accelerate category formation

faq.question: How do researchers test infant categorization?
faq.answer: Using familiarization-novelty preference. Babies are shown many pictures from one category, like cats. Then they see a new cat and a dog. If they look longer at the dog, they have formed a cat category and detect the dog as different. This method works from three months onward.

faq.question: When do labels start helping babies categorize?
faq.answer: By around six months, hearing a consistent label during categorization helps infants form tighter, more coherent categories than visual experience alone. Even before understanding specific words, the presence of a consistent sound signal guides how babies group objects.
